endpoints.interpretation: PFAS, Bisphenol A, inorganic ions, metals, and natural organic matter were co-removed by NF membranes. Membrane selection emphasized simultaneous compliance with drinking water regulations for metals and anions, TOC < 1 mg/L in permeate, and PFAS retention sufficient to lower concentrations from 1700 ng/L feed. NF90 membrane consistently produced permeate meeting legal requirements under all tested compositions, pH values, and pressures; specific PFAS rejection percentages are referred to but not numerically provided in the supplied text.
endpoints.reported_term: co-removal efficiency; retention rates; meeting drinking water standards

endpoints.interpretation: Flux decline with increasing water recovery was attributed to membrane fouling by deposition of humic and fulvic substances and iron on the membrane surface, as well as concentration polarization. Flux increased when feed was diluted at 45% recovery, indicating reversible components of fouling and concentration polarization.

Hydraulic performance was evaluated through permeate flux variation with recovery for A2 and PIII waters. Most membranes experienced decreasing flux as recovery increased toward 80%, with partial flux restoration upon feed dilution, indicating performance impacts from fouling and concentration polarization.

limitations.statement: Experiments were performed on model surface (A2) and groundwater (PIII) compositions rather than on raw natural waters, so matrix complexity and temporal variability of real sources may not be fully captured.

comparability.reason: All permeance measurements in Table 5 were conducted on the same RO membrane architecture (M0–M4) in the same cross-flow setup, reported in identical units (LMH/bar), and with the same PFAS-containing feed, varying only membrane formulation and background constituents. endpoints.interpretation: Pure-water/permeate permeance of PFAS-containing feed through unmodified (M0) and MXene–TiO2-modified (M1–M4) polyamide RO membranes was measured in LMH/bar under different background water compositions (baseline, Ca2+, humic acid, Ca2+-humic acid, CTAB). These data characterize productivity and sensitivity to inorganic, natural organic matter, and surfactant foulants; they do not directly quantify PFAS rejection in the provided text.

PFAS rejection rate R was defined as R(%) = (1 − Cp/Cf) × 100, where Cf and Cp are PFAS feed and permeate concentrations. Although PFAS rejection experiments were conducted for short- and long-chain PFAS (PFOA and PFBA), specific numeric rejection values are not present in the supplied excerpts, so quantitative PFAS removal performance cannot be extracted here.

comparability.reason: Record focuses on PFAS rejection and adsorption in a single FO-PSRNF system treating one groundwater under systematically varied pH and applied pressures; endpoints are consistently reported as rejection (%) and qualitative/ND adsorption for PFAS classes, making within-study comparisons across operating conditions appropriate when conditioning on chain-length grouping and FO operation.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS removal was quantified as rejection efficiency for grouped short- and long-chain PFAS in contaminated groundwater; high rejection was observed at pH 4 and 0 bar.

PFAS adsorption to the PSRNF membrane was analysed for different chain lengths; adsorption decreased with increasing pressure and pH, and was highest for long-chain PFAS at 0 bar. Under alkaline and high-pressure conditions, adsorption of short- and ultrashort-chain species was reported as not detectable.

FTIR analysis indicated greater accumulation of hydrophilic foulants (e.g., NOM, hydrated metal ions) and more intense spectral changes at pH 4 and 0 bar, suggesting higher fouling under acidic conditions; fouling effects were less noticeable at pH 7 and 9.

limitations.statement: Only one membrane type (PSRNF TS80) and one contaminated groundwater source were investigated, which may limit generalizability across other membrane materials and water matrices.
PFAS removal was primarily reported as grouped rejection efficiencies for short- and long-chain classes rather than individual compound-specific rejection values, limiting compound-level comparisons.

endpoints.interpretation: NF-PNIPAm-PVDF membranes showed steady-state rejections of ~70% for PFOA and GenX and ~50% for PFBA at 70 µg/L each PFAS, 2 mM CaCl2, pH ~5.7, T ≈36 °C, 7 bar, and 100 L/m2-h permeate flux in cross-flow; this reflects combined size/charge exclusion and adsorption-driven separation.
endpoints.reported_term: steady-state PFAS rejection and retention under convective flow

endpoints.interpretation: Retention of HFPO-DA (GenX), PFOA, and PFBA over time was monitored in cross-flow cells to assess PFAS separation performance of polymeric NF membranes including NF-PNIPAm-PVDF.

Water permeability (A) of PVDF400, PNIPAm-PVDF, NF-PNIPAm-PVDF, and commercial NF270 membranes was characterized as a function of pressure in cross-flow, showing that adding the NF layer and PNIPAm functionality changes water permeance while still enabling high flux (~100 L/m2-h at 7 bar during PFAS tests).

limitations.statement: Results are limited to model PFAS (PFOA, HFPO-DA, PFBA) at low µg/L concentrations in relatively simple aqueous matrices (type I water with added CaCl2) under bench-scale cross-flow conditions; applicability to complex natural waters or wastewater is not addressed in the reported experiments.
Energy performance is discussed qualitatively ("less energy-intensive" than RO) but no explicit energy consumption metrics are reported for the NF-PNIPAm-PVDF system in the provided excerpts.

endpoints.interpretation: Substantial PFAS sorption occurred to non-adsorbent treatment materials and the membrane. Adsorbed total PFAS mass was dominated by PFOS, with long-chain PFAS exhibiting preferential adsorption. On a mass-normalized basis, the 0.2 µm cartridge filter accumulated the most PFAS, the BW30 membrane and ion exchange (IX) softening resin had similar PFAS accumulation, and greensand accumulated the least. PFAS chain length was the dominant factor for sorption to the filter, membrane, and IX resin, whereas sorption to greensand was more influenced by PFAS functional group.

limitations.statement: Sorption metrics are based on methanol extraction and solid-phase analysis of selected treatment materials from a single pilot CCMS, which may not capture all irreversibly bound PFAS or be fully representative of other systems, materials, or operating histories.

record.citation: Griffin, A.M.; Bellona, C.; Strathmann, T.J. Rejection of PFAS and priority co-contaminants in semiconductor fabrication wastewater by nanofiltration membranes. Water Research 262 (2024) 122111.

comparability.reason: Single-pass NF90 data for TPS and TMAH are generated in a controlled pilot configuration with specified flux, recovery, and pretreatment, enabling comparison of co-contaminant rejection under consistent hydraulic conditions and matrix, though extension to other fluxes, recoveries, or membranes requires caution.

endpoints.interpretation: Percent rejection of fab organic co-contaminants TPS and TMAH based on feed and permeate concentrations at fixed flux and recovery in single-pass pilot operation.

limitations.statement: Rejection of fab co-contaminants TPS and TMAH was assessed at a single flux (25 LMH) and one low single-pass recovery (15%) in pilot single-pass mode, which may not represent performance across the full range of practical operating conditions.

Comparison between lab solution and fab wastewater showed more effective treatment for fab wastewater, but the study used only one fab wastewater composition and particular pretreatment, limiting generalizability.
